title: Christmas Light Installation Invoice Template
subtitle: An invoice pre-filled for holiday lighting jobs — roofline lighting, wreaths, garland, timers, takedown, and rental programs. Download as Excel (auto-calculating), Word, or PDF.
taxHint: Look up your state's sales tax rate
paymentTerms: Net 14 — payment due within 14 days. Late fee of 1.5% per month applies after the due date.
notes: Thank you for your business. Takedown scheduled for early January — weather may shift the date by a few days.
features: Auto-calculating tax formulas in Excel (just enter your state rate)
Pre-filled holiday lighting line items: roofline lighting, wreaths, timers, takedown, labor
Takedown billed on the same invoice — so clients see the full season price up front
License # and EIN / Tax ID fields — required on client-facing invoices in most states

faqs.q: What should I include on a Christmas light installation invoice?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business and contractor license number, the client and job-site address, a dated line-item list (roofline lighting by the foot, wreaths and garland, timers, labor, takedown), tax, and total due. Note the takedown window — most companies schedule removal for early January.

faqs.q: How do I price Christmas light installation?
faqs.a: The most common model is $8–$12 per linear foot for roofline lighting, installed, with materials included. Wreaths, garland, and tree wraps are priced per item, and takedown is either bundled into the per-foot rate or listed as its own line. A 150 ft roofline typically bills $1,350–$1,800 for the full season.

faqs.q: Should takedown be on the same invoice?
faqs.a: Yes — billing install, materials, and takedown on one invoice avoids disputes in January. If you run a rental program (you own the lights), list the season as a single package line instead and note that the lights remain your property.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate tax automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, tax and total update automatically. Leave the tax rate blank if you are not required to charge sales tax.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

deepDive.heading: Christmas light invoices: price the season, then bill the takedown
deepDive.sub: Holiday lighting is the one trade where the work is finished in December and the job is not over until January. The invoice has to anticipate that.

blocks.h3: Price the season, not the night
paras: A Christmas light install is priced on two axes: the length of roofline you cover, and the access difficulty of the property. Per-foot rates sit around $3-$8 per linear foot installed for standard single-story eave work, and climb quickly on steep pitches, two-story gables and metal roofs where clips behave differently. Wrapping trees prices by height instead: roughly $100-$300 per tree depending on trunk height and density.

Turn that into three packages rather than a per-foot quote, because homeowners compare packages. A roofline-only tier, a roofline-plus-trees tier, and a full-property tier including wreaths, garland and controller setup.
list: Roofline only, single story: commonly $500-$1,200 per home
Roofline plus trees and bushes: roughly $1,200-$2,500
Full property with wreaths, garland, controller and timer: $2,500 and up
Minimum call-out: many installers set $250-$400, and it belongs on the invoice as its own line
Cite the linear feet measured on the invoice — it is the number a customer can verify against their own house

blocks.h3: The takedown is a separate job on the same invoice
paras: Most holiday lighting disputes are not about the install price. They are about the takedown: whether it was included, when it happens, and who owns the product afterwards. Put the takedown on the invoice as a scheduled line with its own date window, even when it is bundled into the season price.

If you store the lights for the customer, that is a third line, and it is also the reason some installers retain repeat business. If the customer keeps a mix of their own lights and yours, record which is which before the truck leaves.
list: Takedown window stated as a date range, not "after the holidays"
Takedown priced separately: commonly $150-$400 depending on property size
Storage line if you keep the material between seasons
Ownership noted per item: customer-supplied lights vs. installer inventory
Mid-season repair call-outs quoted as their own rate — a strand going dark in week two is not a warranty claim if the customer's own lights were used

blocks.h3: What to record before you leave the property
paras: Holiday lighting runs on ladders and roofs in the coldest month of the year, often on pre-existing gutters that are already at the end of their life. The invoice is a record of what you found, not only what you installed.
A short condition note protects both sides and takes under a minute to write.
list: Existing gutter, soffit and fascia condition noted where clips or hangers were attached
Outdoor outlet and circuit used — especially where the customer has no exterior power and a cord runs through a window
Photo of the finished install attached to the job record
Weather-cancelled days noted, since rescheduling is the most common source of a rate dispute
Customer approval of the light layout before install, in writing or by message
